sections.text:
Someone objects that other beings are sometimes numbered together with the Father and the Son without therefore being glorified together with them. Paul, for example, includes angels in his solemn charge to Timothy: “I charge you before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels.” We do not remove angels from the rest of creation, yet neither do we consent to count them together with Father and Son in the same divine rank.

Although the objection scarcely deserves an answer because its absurdity is so evident, I say this: before a just and gentle judge one may bring even a fellow-servant as witness, especially when the judge wishes to display the unquestionable justice of his decisions. But to make a slave free, call a person a child of God, and give life from death belongs only to the One who has a natural relation to God and is himself free from the condition of servitude. How could one who is alien make us God's own? How could one under the yoke of slavery free another?

Therefore the mention of the Spirit and the mention of angels are not made in the same way. The Spirit is invoked as the living Lord; angels are brought forward as fellow-servants who assist and as faithful witnesses of the truth.

The saints commonly deliver God's commands in the presence of witnesses. Paul tells Timothy: “What you received from me in the presence of many witnesses, entrust these things to faithful people.” Now he calls angels as witnesses because he knows that angels will accompany Christ when he comes in the glory of the Father to judge the world in righteousness. The Lord says: “Whoever confesses me before human beings, the Son of Man will confess before the angels of God; but the one who denies me before human beings will be denied before the angels of God.” Paul likewise speaks of “the revelation of the Lord Jesus from heaven with his angels.”

Thus Paul calls the angels to witness now, preparing testimony for the great judgment.

Nor is Paul alone in doing this. Those entrusted with the stewardship of souls repeatedly call witnesses to what they teach. They even call heaven and earth to witness, because every human action takes place within them and because, at the examination of our deeds, creation itself stands as witness.

Thus it is written: “He will call heaven above and the earth, that he may judge his people.” Moses, about to deliver God's words, says, “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today.” In his song he says, “Give ear, O heavens, and I will speak; let the earth hear the words of my mouth.” Isaiah likewise says, “Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth,” and Jeremiah describes heaven as astonished at the people's evil.

Joshua son of Nun even set up a stone as witness to his words, saying, “This stone shall be a witness against you,” perhaps trusting that by God's power even stones could raise a voice against transgressors—or at least that each person's conscience would be pierced by the force of the reminder.

In this way those charged with the care of souls prepare witnesses, whatever their kind, to stand for a future accounting. But the Spirit is ranked with God not because of a temporary need for testimony, but because of natural communion. He was not dragged into the rank by us; he was placed there by the Lord.

translator_notes: Basil distinguishes angels as created witnesses/fellow-servants from the Holy Spirit as Lord and life-giver.
The section uses courtroom and covenant imagery to explain Paul's appeal to angels.
